about: Which IP addresses are on the public internet, as easybrandkit and easyscreenshotkit judge them and as MakersMCP-Api's helpers/kits/fetch-input.js judges them since aaae809. Every IPv6 form that holds an IPv4 address (mapped, compatible, translated, 6to4 and NAT64's well known prefix) is judged by the IPv4 address it holds. notPublic holds addresses of this machine, of private, shared and link-local networks and of the special IPv4 ranges, and in IPv6 of Teredo (2001::/32), NAT64's local use prefix (64:ff9b:1::/48), the discard range 100::/64, the documentation range 2001:db8::/32, the site local range and multicast. public holds, among the rest, IPv6's newer documentation range 3fff::/20 and its benchmarking range 2001:2::/48, which the kits and MakersMCP-Api count as public. publicInKitsOnly lists NAT64 addresses of public sites: the kits judge them by the IPv4 address they hold, so a site with IPv4 only stays public on a network with IPv6 only, where MakersMCP-Api refuses NAT64's well known prefix whole, as the kits firewall does. reachesLoopback lists, by the address of this machine's loopback a connection to each reaches, addresses that MAKERSMCP_REFUSE_ADDRESSES judges as that address as well: 0.0.0.0 in each of its forms reaches 127.0.0.1 and :: reaches ::1, so a setting that refuses 127.0.0.1 refuses each address of the first list, and one that refuses ::1 each of the second, and neither the other's; reachesLoopbackHosts lists the same as the host of an address is written, 0.0.0.0 as 0, 0x0 or 0.0 too, each as the address given and as a page's. theHostGiven lists, for an address given at this machine's own names, the addresses on its port that are the host given too, each opened from it: where the host given is localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1], and where it is 127.0.0.1 or [::1], localhost. notTheHostGiven lists, for an address given on this machine or a private network, addresses that are not the host given though they lead to an address of it, each refused from it as not on the public internet, for many sites are served at one address and port, a program there picking each by its name: a name a hosts file answers with the address of a loopback host given, a name of the public DNS that answers with 127.0.0.1, as every name under ddev.site does, a name at the address of a private host given, a name under localhost, which a router on this machine serves as a site of its own, the addresses of a host given by its name, another address of 127.0.0.0/8, 0.0.0.0 and ::, and from 127.0.0.1 the address [::1] and from [::1] 127.0.0.1, which reach this machine as well but no address of each other, and can be two programs on one port; names holds what the system's lookup answers for each name of a case, localhost and the names under it answered by the kits themselves.
